{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q313745]] Wikidata name: Tokugawa Tsunayoshi [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 09:59, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Short description|Japanese shogun}} {{Infobox Officeholder | name = Tokugawa Tsunayoshi | title = ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' | image = Tsunyaoshi.jpg | caption = Tokugawa Tsunayoshi | term = 1680–1709 | monarch = {{Plainlist| * [[:en:Emperor Reigen|Reigen]] * [[:en:Emperor Higashiyama|Higashiyama]]}} | predecessor = [[:en:Tokugawa Ietsuna|Tokugawa Ietsuna]] | successor = [[:en:Tokugawa Ienobu|Tokugawa Ienobu]] | children = {{plainlist| * Tsuruhime * [[Tokugawa Tokumatsu]] * [[Kichihime]] * [[Yaehime]] * [[Takehime (Tokugawa)|Takehime]] }} |birth_date = {{birth date|1646|2|23|df=y}} |birth_place = [[:en:Edo|Edo]], [[Tokugawa shogunate]]
(now [[:en:Tokyo|Tokyo]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]) | death_date = {{death date and age|1709|02|19|1646|02|23|df=y}} | death_place = Edo, Tokugawa shogunate | parents = [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]]
[[Keishouin]] | signature = Tokugawa Tsunayoshi kao.jpg | spouse = {{ill|Takatsukasa Nobuko|ja|鷹司信子|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takatsukasa Nobuko|qq=}} }} {{family name hatnote|[[Tokugawa (surname)|Tokugawa]]|lang=Japanese}} {{nihongo|'''Tokugawa Tsunayoshi'''|徳川 綱吉||extra=February 23, 1646 – February 19, 1709}} was the fifth ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' of the [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa dynasty]] of Japan. He was the younger brother of [[:en:Tokugawa Ietsuna|Tokugawa Ietsuna]], as well as the son of [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]], the grandson of [[:en:Tokugawa Hidetada|Tokugawa Hidetada]], and the great-grandson of [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]].Nussbaum, Louis-Frédéric. (2005). "''Tokugawa, Tsunayoshi''" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|''Japan Encyclopedia'', p. 979|page=979}}; n.b., Louis-Frédéric is pseudonym of Louis-Frédéric Nussbaum, ''see'' [http://dispatch.opac.ddb.de/DB=4.1/PPN?PPN=128842709 Deutsche Nationalbibliothek Authority File] {{Webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20120524174828/http://dispatch.opac.ddb.de/DB=4.1/PPN?PPN=128842709 |date=2012-05-24 }}. Tsunayoshi is known for instituting animal protection laws, particularly for dogs. This earned him the nickname of "the dog ''Shogun''" (''Inu-Kubō'' 犬公方: ''Inu=''Dog, ''Kubō''=formal title of Shogun). ==Early years (1646–1680)== [[File:Keishōin.jpg|thumb|106px|Keishōin, Tsunayoshi's mother]] Tokugawa Tsunayoshi was born on February 23, 1646, in Edo. He was the son of [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]] by one of his concubines, named Otama, later known as Keishōin 桂昌院 (1627–1705). Tsunayoshi had an elder brother already five years old, who would become the next shogun after Iemitsu's death, [[:en:Tokugawa Ietsuna|Tokugawa Ietsuna]]. Tsunayoshi was born in [[:en:Edo|Edo]] and after his birth moved in with his mother to her own private apartments in [[:en:Edo Castle|Edo Castle]]. "The younger son (Tsunayoshi) apparently distinguished himself by his precociousness and liveliness at an early age, and the father, the third shogun, Iemitsu, became fearful that he might usurp the position of his duller elder brothers [and] thus he ordered that the boy (Tsunayoshi) not to be brought up as a samurai/warrior, as was becoming for his station, but be trained as a scholar."{{attribution needed|date=January 2018}}Bodart-Bailey, B., ed. (1999). ''Kaempfer's Japan: Tokugawa Japan Observed'', citing Buya shokudan, in Kokushi sosho, edited by Kokushi Kenkyu Kai (Tokyo 1917), ser. 2, 86–87. His childhood name was Tokumatsu ({{lang|ja|徳松}}). While his father was ''shōgun'', his mother was an adopted daughter of the [[Honjō family]], led by [[Honjō Munemasa]] (1580–1639) in Kyoto. His mother's natural parents were merchants in Kyoto. This remarkable woman was very close with Tsunayoshi in his young years, and while his older brother Ietsuna began to rely on regents for much of his reign, Tsunayoshi did exactly the opposite, relying on his remarkable mother for advice until her death. In 1651, ''shōgun'' Iemitsu died when Tsunayoshi was only five years old. His older brother, Tokugawa Ietsuna, became shogun. For the most part, Tsunayoshi's life during the reign of his brother ''shōgun'' Ietsuna is unknown, but he never advised his brother. ==Family== * Father: [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]] (August 12, 1604 – June 8, 1651) * Mother: Otama no Kata ({{lang|ja|玉方}},{{cite web |title=「桂昌院」の意味・読み・例文・類語 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%A1%82%E6%98%8C%E9%99%A2-16051 |website=コトバンク |date=13 May 2016 |publisher=日本国語大辞典 |access-date=28 October 2023}} 1627–1705) later {{ill|Keishōin|ja|桂昌院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keishōin|qq=}}, daughter of {{ill|Honjo Munemasa|ja|本庄宗正|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honjo Munemasa|qq=}} * Wife: Takatsukasa Nobuko (1651–1709) later Jokoin, daughter of court noble [[:en:Takatsukasa Norihira|Takatsukasa Norihira]] * Concubines: ** Oden no Kata (1658–1738) later {{ill|Zuishun-in|ja|瑞春院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zuishun-in|qq=}} ** {{ill|Lady Emonosuke|ja|寿光院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lady Emonosuke|qq=}} (d. 1705) ** Lady Osuke (d. 1714) later Jukoin ** Lady Shinsuke, later {{ill|Sheishin-in|ja|清心院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sheishin-in|qq=}} * Children: ** Tsuruhime (1677–1704) by Oden, married Tokugawa Tsunanori of [[:en:Kii Domain|Kii Domain]] ** Tokugawa Tokumatsu (1679–1683), [[:en:Tatebayashi Domain|Tatebayashi Domain]] by Oden * Adopted: ** [[:en:Tokugawa Ienobu|Tokugawa Ienobu]] ** Kichihime (1697–1701) signed as Midaidokoro's daughter ** Yaehime (1689–1746) daughter of [[:en:Takatsukasa Sukenobu|Takatsukasa Sukenobu]], married [[Tokugawa Yoshizane]] of Mito Family later Yousen-in had 1 daughter, Miyohime married [[:en:Tokugawa Munetaka|Tokugawa Munetaka]] signed as Midaidokoro's daughter ** Matsuhime daughter of [[:en:Tokugawa Tsunanari|Tokugawa Tsunanari]] married [[:en:Maeda Yoshinori|Maeda Yoshinori]] signed as Midaidokoro's daughter ** Takehime (1705–1772), daughter of Hirosada Seikan'in and adopted by [[:en:Tokugawa Yoshimune|Tokugawa Yoshimune]] and married [[Shimazu Tsugutoyo]] of [[:en:Satsuma Domain|Satsuma Domain]] and known as Joganin had 1 daughter, Kikuhime (1733–1808) signed as Midaidokoro's daughter and signed as Okume no Kata's daughter when she became adopted daughter of Yoshimune ==Disputed succession (1680)== In 1680, ''shōgun'' Ietsuna died at the premature age of 38. * '''June 4, 1680''' (''[[:en:Enpō|Enpō]] 8, 8th day of the 5th month''): Shogun Ietsuna's death leads to the accession of Tsunayoshi as head of the shogunate.Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). ''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 414. * '''1680–81''' (''Enpō 8''): [[:en:Gokoku-ji|Gokoku-ji]] in Edo is founded in honor of Tsunayoshi's mother. * '''1681''' (''[[:en:Tenna|Tenna]] 1''): Tsunayoshi's investiture as ''shōgun''. A power struggle ensued, and for a time, the succession remained an open question. [[:en:Sakai Tadakiyo|Sakai Tadakiyo]], one of Ietsuna's most favored advisors, suggested that the succession not pass to someone of the Tokugawa line, but rather to the blood royal, favoring one of the sons of [[:en:Emperor Go-Sai|Emperor Go-Sai]] to become the next ''shōgun'' (as during the [[:en:Kamakura shogunate|Kamakura shogunate]]) but Tadakiyo was dismissed soon after. [[:en:Hotta Masatoshi|Hotta Masatoshi]], one of the most brilliant advisors of ''shōgun'' Ietsuna's rule, was the first person to suggest that Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, as the brother of the former ''shōgun'' and the son of the third, become the next ''shōgun''. Finally, in 1681 (''Tenna 1''), Tsunayoshi's elevation was confirmed; and he was installed as the fifth ''shōgun'' of the Tokugawa shogunate. ==''Shōgun'' (1680–1709)== {{Unreferenced section|date=December 2022}} Immediately after becoming ''shōgun'', Tsunayoshi gave [[:en:Hotta Masatoshi|Hotta Masatoshi]] the title of ''[[:en:Tairō|Tairō]]'', in a way thanking him for ensuring his succession. Almost immediately after he became shogun, he ordered a vassal of the [[:en:Takada Domain|Takata]] to commit suicide because of misgovernment, showing his strict approach to the samurai code. He then confiscated his fief of 250,000 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]''. During his reign, he confiscated a total of 1,400,000 ''koku''. In 1682, ''shōgun'' Tsunayoshi ordered his censors and police to raise the living standard of the people. Soon, prostitution was banned, waitresses could not be employed in tea houses, and rare and expensive fabrics were banned. Most probably, smuggling began as a practice in Japan soon after Tsunayoshi's authoritarian laws came into effect. In 1684, Tsunayoshi also decreased the power of the ''tairō'' after the assassination of Masatoshi by a cousin in that same year. Nonetheless, due again to maternal advice, Tsunayoshi became very religious, promoting the [[:en:Neo-Confucianism|Neo-Confucianism]] of [[:en:Zhu Xi|Zhu Xi]]. In 1682, he read to the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]s'' an exposition of the "Great Learning", which became an annual tradition at the ''shōgun''{{'}}s court. He soon began to lecture even more, and in 1690 lectured about Neo-Confucian work to [[Shinto]] and [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] ''daimyōs'', and even to envoys from the court of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Higashiyama|Higashiyama]] in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. He also was interested in several Chinese works, namely ''The Great Learning'' ([[:en:Da Xue|Da Xue]]) and ''The Classic of Filial Piety'' ([[:en:Xiao Jing|Xiao Jing]]). Tsunayoshi also loved art and [[:en:Noh|Noh]] theater. In 1691, [[:en:Engelbert Kaempfer|Engelbert Kaempfer]] visited Edo as part of the annual [[:en:Dutch missions to Edo|Dutch embassy]] from [[:en:Dejima|Dejima]] in [[:en:Nagasaki|Nagasaki]]. He journeyed from Nagasaki to [[:en:Osaka|Osaka]], to [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], and there to [[:en:Edo|Edo]]. Kaempfer gives us information on Japan during the early reign of Tokugawa Tsunayoshi. As the Dutch embassy entered Edo in 1692, they asked to have an audience with Shogun Tsunayoshi. While they were waiting for approval, a fire destroyed six hundred houses in Edo, and the audience was postponed. Tsunayoshi and several of the ladies of the court sat behind reed screens, while the Dutch embassy sat in front of them. Tsunayoshi took an interest in Western matters, and apparently asked them to talk and sing with one another for him to see how Westerners behaved. Tsunayoshi later put on a Noh drama for them. [[File:Nakano Inugoya dog shelters 1696.png|thumb|Nakano Inugoya (Nakano dog shelters) in 1696. Tsunayoshi built large kennels in Nakano, Yotsuya and Okubo in Edo (Tokyo). Even during the famine the Shogunate accommodated 80,000 wild dogs in the kennels in Nakano and gave them 3 go (0.18L) of polished rice, 50 moon (187g) of bean paste and 1 go of sardines daily. The total space for the dog shelters in Nakano was approximately 750,000 square meters in 1702.[https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1178647/63 中野犬小屋本論]『武蔵野歴史地理. 第2冊』高橋源一郎編, 武蔵野歴史地理学会, 1928, p58-96]] Owing to religious fundamentalism, Tsunayoshi sought protection for living beings in the later parts of his rule. In the 1690s and first decade of the 1700s, Tsunayoshi, who was born in the Year of the Dog, thought he should take several measures concerning dogs. A collection of edicts released daily, known as the {{nihongo|''Edicts on Compassion for Living Things''|生類憐みの令|Shōruiawareminorei|}}, told the populace, among other things, to protect dogs, since in Edo there were many stray and diseased dogs walking around the city. Therefore, he earned the pejorative title ''Inu-Kubō'' (犬公方: ''Inu=''Dog, ''Kubō''=formal title of Shogun). In 1695, there were so many dogs that Edo began to smell horribly. An apprentice was even executed because he wounded a dog. Finally, the issue was taken to an extreme, as over 50,000 dogs were deported to kennels in the suburbs of the city where they would be housed. They were apparently fed rice and fish at the expense of the taxpaying citizens of Edo. For the latter part of Tsunayoshi's reign, he was advised by [[:en:Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu|Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu]]. It was a golden era of classic Japanese art, known as the ''[[:en:Genroku|Genroku]] era''. In 1701, [[:en:Asano Naganori|Asano Naganori]], the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Akō Domain|Akō]] han, having been allegedly insulted by [[:en:Kira Yoshinaka|Kira Yoshinaka]] in [[:en:Edo Castle|Edo Castle]], attempted to kill him. Asano was executed, but Kira went unpunished. Asano's [[:en:Forty-seven rōnin|forty-seven ''rōnin'']] avenged his death by killing Kira and became a legend that influenced many plays and stories of the era. The most successful of them was a [[:en:Bunraku|Bunraku]] play called ''Kanadehon Chūshingura'' (now simply called ''[[:en:Chūshingura|Chūshingura]]'', or "Treasury of Loyal Retainers"), written in 1748 by [[Takeda Izumo]] and two associates; it was later adapted into a [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] play, which is still one of Japan's most popular. The earliest known account of the Akō incident in the West was published in 1822 in [[:en:Isaac Titsingh|Isaac Titsingh]]'s book, ''Illustrations of Japan''.Screech, Timon. (2006). ''Secret Memoirs of the Shoguns: Isaac Titsingh and Japan, 1779–1822'', p. 91. Tsunayoshi's first son Tokugawa Tokumatsu (1679–1683) died at the age of 4 due to illness. In 1704, Tsunayoshi's only surviving child, Tsuruhime died following a miscarriage and a few months after her{{whose|date=September 2024}} husband, his son-in-law, Tokugawa Tsunanori of [[:en:Kii Domain|Kii Domain]] also died. Therefore, Tsunayoshi appointed his nephew, [[:en:Tokugawa Ienobu|Tokugawa Ienobu]], heir apparent in the winter of 1704. Ienobu was the son of his other brother, [[:en:Tokugawa Tsunashige|Tokugawa Tsunashige]], the former Lord of [[:en:Kōfu|Kōfu]], which was a title Ienobu held himself before becoming ''shōgun''. Ienobu moved into the official residence of Shogunal heir apparent at the [[Edo_Castle#Ninomaru|Western Perimeter of Edo Castle]]. In 1706, Edo was hit by a typhoon, and [[:en:Mount Fuji|Mount Fuji]] erupted the following year. ==Death== It was insinuated that Tsunayoshi was stabbed by his consort after he tried to proclaim an illegitimate child as his heir; this concept, stemming from the [[Sanno Gaiki]], is refuted in contemporary records which explain that Tsunayoshi had the measles at the end of his life and died on February 19, 1709, in the presence of his entourage.Bodart-Bailey, p. 165. His death was just four days short of his 63rd birthday. He was given the Buddhist name Joken'in ({{lang|ja|常憲院}}) and buried in [[Kan'ei-ji]]. ==Eras of Tsunayoshi's ''bakufu''== The years in which Tsunayoshi was shogun are more specifically identified by more than one [[:en:Japanese era names|era name]] or ''[[:en:Nengō|Nengō]]''.Titsingh, pp. 414–415. * ''[[:en:Enpō|Enpō]]'' (1673–1681) * ''[[:en:Tenna|Tenna]]'' (1681–1684) * ''[[:en:Jōkyō|Jōkyō]]'' (1684–1688) * ''[[:en:Genroku|Genroku]]'' (1688–1704) * ''[[:en:Hōei|Hōei]]'' (1704–1711) ==Ancestry== {{ahnentafel |collapsed=yes |align=center |ref={{cite web|url=https://reichsarchiv.jp/%e5%ae%b6%e7%b3%bb%e3%83%aa%e3%82%b9%e3%83%88/%e5%be%b3%e5%b7%9d%ef%bc%88%e5%be%b7%e5%b7%9d%ef%bc%89%e6%b0%8f%ef%bc%88%e5%b0%86%e8%bb%8d%e5%ae%b6%ef%bc%89#tunayosi|title=Genealogy|website=Reichsarchiv|access-date=4 July 2018|language=ja}} |boxstyle_1=background-color: #fcc; |boxstyle_2=background-color: #fb9; |boxstyle_3=background-color: #ffc; |boxstyle_4=background-color: #bfc; |1= 1. '''Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, 5th [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa Shōgun]]''' |2= 2. [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]], 3rd [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa Shōgun]] (1604-1651) |3= 3. (now [[:en:Tokyo|Tokyo]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]) | death_date = {{death date and age|1709|02|19|1646|02|23|df=y}} | death_place = Edo, Tokugawa shogunate | parents = [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]]
[[Keishouin]] | signature = Tokugawa Tsunayoshi kao.jpg | spouse = {{ill|Takatsukasa Nobuko|ja|鷹司信子|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takatsukasa Nobuko|qq=}} }} {{family name hatnote|[[Tokugawa (surname)|Tokugawa]]|lang=Japanese}} {{nihongo|'''Tokugawa Tsunayoshi'''|徳川 綱吉||extra=February 23, 1646 – February 19, 1709}} was the fifth ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' of the [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa dynasty]] of Japan. He was the younger brother of [[:en:Tokugawa Ietsuna|Tokugawa Ietsuna]], as well as the son of [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]], the grandson of [[:en:Tokugawa Hidetada|Tokugawa Hidetada]], and the great-grandson of [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]].Nussbaum, Louis-Frédéric. (2005). "''Tokugawa, Tsunayoshi''" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|''Japan Encyclopedia'', p. 979|page=979}}; n.b., Louis-Frédéric is pseudonym of Louis-Frédéric Nussbaum, ''see'' [http://dispatch.opac.ddb.de/DB=4.1/PPN?PPN=128842709 Deutsche Nationalbibliothek Authority File] {{Webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20120524174828/http://dispatch.opac.ddb.de/DB=4.1/PPN?PPN=128842709 |date=2012-05-24 }}. Tsunayoshi is known for instituting animal protection laws, particularly for dogs. This earned him the nickname of "the dog ''Shogun''" (''Inu-Kubō'' 犬公方: ''Inu=''Dog, ''Kubō''=formal title of Shogun). ==Early years (1646–1680)== [[File:Keishōin.jpg|thumb|106px|Keishōin, Tsunayoshi's mother]] Tokugawa Tsunayoshi was born on February 23, 1646, in Edo. He was the son of [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]] by one of his concubines, named Otama, later known as Keishōin 桂昌院 (1627–1705). Tsunayoshi had an elder brother already five years old, who would become the next shogun after Iemitsu's death, [[:en:Tokugawa Ietsuna|Tokugawa Ietsuna]]. Tsunayoshi was born in [[:en:Edo|Edo]] and after his birth moved in with his mother to her own private apartments in [[:en:Edo Castle|Edo Castle]]. "The younger son (Tsunayoshi) apparently distinguished himself by his precociousness and liveliness at an early age, and the father, the third shogun, Iemitsu, became fearful that he might usurp the position of his duller elder brothers [and] thus he ordered that the boy (Tsunayoshi) not to be brought up as a samurai/warrior, as was becoming for his station, but be trained as a scholar."{{attribution needed|date=January 2018}}Bodart-Bailey, B., ed. (1999). ''Kaempfer's Japan: Tokugawa Japan Observed'', citing Buya shokudan, in Kokushi sosho, edited by Kokushi Kenkyu Kai (Tokyo 1917), ser. 2, 86–87. His childhood name was Tokumatsu ({{lang|ja|徳松}}). While his father was ''shōgun'', his mother was an adopted daughter of the [[Honjō family]], led by [[Honjō Munemasa]] (1580–1639) in Kyoto. His mother's natural parents were merchants in Kyoto. This remarkable woman was very close with Tsunayoshi in his young years, and while his older brother Ietsuna began to rely on regents for much of his reign, Tsunayoshi did exactly the opposite, relying on his remarkable mother for advice until her death. In 1651, ''shōgun'' Iemitsu died when Tsunayoshi was only five years old. His older brother, Tokugawa Ietsuna, became shogun. For the most part, Tsunayoshi's life during the reign of his brother ''shōgun'' Ietsuna is unknown, but he never advised his brother. ==Family== * Father: [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]] (August 12, 1604 – June 8, 1651) * Mother: Otama no Kata ({{lang|ja|玉方}},{{cite web |title=「桂昌院」の意味・読み・例文・類語 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%A1%82%E6%98%8C%E9%99%A2-16051 |website=コトバンク |date=13 May 2016 |publisher=日本国語大辞典 |access-date=28 October 2023}} 1627–1705) later {{ill|Keishōin|ja|桂昌院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keishōin|qq=}}, daughter of {{ill|Honjo Munemasa|ja|本庄宗正|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honjo Munemasa|qq=}} * Wife: Takatsukasa Nobuko (1651–1709) later Jokoin, daughter of court noble [[:en:Takatsukasa Norihira|Takatsukasa Norihira]] * Concubines: ** Oden no Kata (1658–1738) later {{ill|Zuishun-in|ja|瑞春院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zuishun-in|qq=}} ** {{ill|Lady Emonosuke|ja|寿光院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lady Emonosuke|qq=}} (d. 1705) ** Lady Osuke (d. 1714) later Jukoin ** Lady Shinsuke, later {{ill|Sheishin-in|ja|清心院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sheishin-in|qq=}} * Children: ** Tsuruhime (1677–1704) by Oden, married Tokugawa Tsunanori of [[:en:Kii Domain|Kii Domain]] ** Tokugawa Tokumatsu (1679–1683), [[:en:Tatebayashi Domain|Tatebayashi Domain]] by Oden * Adopted: ** [[:en:Tokugawa Ienobu|Tokugawa Ienobu]] ** Kichihime (1697–1701) signed as Midaidokoro's daughter ** Yaehime (1689–1746) daughter of [[:en:Takatsukasa Sukenobu|Takatsukasa Sukenobu]], married [[Tokugawa Yoshizane]] of Mito Family later Yousen-in had 1 daughter, Miyohime married [[:en:Tokugawa Munetaka|Tokugawa Munetaka]] signed as Midaidokoro's daughter ** Matsuhime daughter of [[:en:Tokugawa Tsunanari|Tokugawa Tsunanari]] married [[:en:Maeda Yoshinori|Maeda Yoshinori]] signed as Midaidokoro's daughter ** Takehime (1705–1772), daughter of Hirosada Seikan'in and adopted by [[:en:Tokugawa Yoshimune|Tokugawa Yoshimune]] and married [[Shimazu Tsugutoyo]] of [[:en:Satsuma Domain|Satsuma Domain]] and known as Joganin had 1 daughter, Kikuhime (1733–1808) signed as Midaidokoro's daughter and signed as Okume no Kata's daughter when she became adopted daughter of Yoshimune ==Disputed succession (1680)== In 1680, ''shōgun'' Ietsuna died at the premature age of 38. * '''June 4, 1680''' (''[[:en:Enpō|Enpō]] 8, 8th day of the 5th month''): Shogun Ietsuna's death leads to the accession of Tsunayoshi as head of the shogunate.Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). ''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 414. * '''1680–81''' (''Enpō 8''): [[:en:Gokoku-ji|Gokoku-ji]] in Edo is founded in honor of Tsunayoshi's mother. * '''1681''' (''[[:en:Tenna|Tenna]] 1''): Tsunayoshi's investiture as ''shōgun''. A power struggle ensued, and for a time, the succession remained an open question. [[:en:Sakai Tadakiyo|Sakai Tadakiyo]], one of Ietsuna's most favored advisors, suggested that the succession not pass to someone of the Tokugawa line, but rather to the blood royal, favoring one of the sons of [[:en:Emperor Go-Sai|Emperor Go-Sai]] to become the next ''shōgun'' (as during the [[:en:Kamakura shogunate|Kamakura shogunate]]) but Tadakiyo was dismissed soon after. [[:en:Hotta Masatoshi|Hotta Masatoshi]], one of the most brilliant advisors of ''shōgun'' Ietsuna's rule, was the first person to suggest that Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, as the brother of the former ''shōgun'' and the son of the third, become the next ''shōgun''. Finally, in 1681 (''Tenna 1''), Tsunayoshi's elevation was confirmed; and he was installed as the fifth ''shōgun'' of the Tokugawa shogunate. ==''Shōgun'' (1680–1709)== {{Unreferenced section|date=December 2022}} Immediately after becoming ''shōgun'', Tsunayoshi gave [[:en:Hotta Masatoshi|Hotta Masatoshi]] the title of ''[[:en:Tairō|Tairō]]'', in a way thanking him for ensuring his succession. Almost immediately after he became shogun, he ordered a vassal of the [[:en:Takada Domain|Takata]] to commit suicide because of misgovernment, showing his strict approach to the samurai code. He then confiscated his fief of 250,000 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]''. During his reign, he confiscated a total of 1,400,000 ''koku''. In 1682, ''shōgun'' Tsunayoshi ordered his censors and police to raise the living standard of the people. Soon, prostitution was banned, waitresses could not be employed in tea houses, and rare and expensive fabrics were banned. Most probably, smuggling began as a practice in Japan soon after Tsunayoshi's authoritarian laws came into effect. In 1684, Tsunayoshi also decreased the power of the ''tairō'' after the assassination of Masatoshi by a cousin in that same year. Nonetheless, due again to maternal advice, Tsunayoshi became very religious, promoting the [[:en:Neo-Confucianism|Neo-Confucianism]] of [[:en:Zhu Xi|Zhu Xi]]. In 1682, he read to the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]s'' an exposition of the "Great Learning", which became an annual tradition at the ''shōgun''{{'}}s court. He soon began to lecture even more, and in 1690 lectured about Neo-Confucian work to [[Shinto]] and [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] ''daimyōs'', and even to envoys from the court of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Higashiyama|Higashiyama]] in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. He also was interested in several Chinese works, namely ''The Great Learning'' ([[:en:Da Xue|Da Xue]]) and ''The Classic of Filial Piety'' ([[:en:Xiao Jing|Xiao Jing]]). Tsunayoshi also loved art and [[:en:Noh|Noh]] theater. In 1691, [[:en:Engelbert Kaempfer|Engelbert Kaempfer]] visited Edo as part of the annual [[:en:Dutch missions to Edo|Dutch embassy]] from [[:en:Dejima|Dejima]] in [[:en:Nagasaki|Nagasaki]]. He journeyed from Nagasaki to [[:en:Osaka|Osaka]], to [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], and there to [[:en:Edo|Edo]]. Kaempfer gives us information on Japan during the early reign of Tokugawa Tsunayoshi. As the Dutch embassy entered Edo in 1692, they asked to have an audience with Shogun Tsunayoshi. While they were waiting for approval, a fire destroyed six hundred houses in Edo, and the audience was postponed. Tsunayoshi and several of the ladies of the court sat behind reed screens, while the Dutch embassy sat in front of them. Tsunayoshi took an interest in Western matters, and apparently asked them to talk and sing with one another for him to see how Westerners behaved. Tsunayoshi later put on a Noh drama for them. [[File:Nakano Inugoya dog shelters 1696.png|thumb|Nakano Inugoya (Nakano dog shelters) in 1696. Tsunayoshi built large kennels in Nakano, Yotsuya and Okubo in Edo (Tokyo). Even during the famine the Shogunate accommodated 80,000 wild dogs in the kennels in Nakano and gave them 3 go (0.18L) of polished rice, 50 moon (187g) of bean paste and 1 go of sardines daily. The total space for the dog shelters in Nakano was approximately 750,000 square meters in 1702.[https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1178647/63 中野犬小屋本論]『武蔵野歴史地理. 第2冊』高橋源一郎編, 武蔵野歴史地理学会, 1928, p58-96]] Owing to religious fundamentalism, Tsunayoshi sought protection for living beings in the later parts of his rule. In the 1690s and first decade of the 1700s, Tsunayoshi, who was born in the Year of the Dog, thought he should take several measures concerning dogs. A collection of edicts released daily, known as the {{nihongo|''Edicts on Compassion for Living Things''|生類憐みの令|Shōruiawareminorei|}}, told the populace, among other things, to protect dogs, since in Edo there were many stray and diseased dogs walking around the city. Therefore, he earned the pejorative title ''Inu-Kubō'' (犬公方: ''Inu=''Dog, ''Kubō''=formal title of Shogun). In 1695, there were so many dogs that Edo began to smell horribly. An apprentice was even executed because he wounded a dog. Finally, the issue was taken to an extreme, as over 50,000 dogs were deported to kennels in the suburbs of the city where they would be housed. They were apparently fed rice and fish at the expense of the taxpaying citizens of Edo. For the latter part of Tsunayoshi's reign, he was advised by [[:en:Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu|Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu]]. It was a golden era of classic Japanese art, known as the ''[[:en:Genroku|Genroku]] era''. In 1701, [[:en:Asano Naganori|Asano Naganori]], the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Akō Domain|Akō]] han, having been allegedly insulted by [[:en:Kira Yoshinaka|Kira Yoshinaka]] in [[:en:Edo Castle|Edo Castle]], attempted to kill him. Asano was executed, but Kira went unpunished. Asano's [[:en:Forty-seven rōnin|forty-seven ''rōnin'']] avenged his death by killing Kira and became a legend that influenced many plays and stories of the era. The most successful of them was a [[:en:Bunraku|Bunraku]] play called ''Kanadehon Chūshingura'' (now simply called ''[[:en:Chūshingura|Chūshingura]]'', or "Treasury of Loyal Retainers"), written in 1748 by [[Takeda Izumo]] and two associates; it was later adapted into a [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] play, which is still one of Japan's most popular. The earliest known account of the Akō incident in the West was published in 1822 in [[:en:Isaac Titsingh|Isaac Titsingh]]'s book, ''Illustrations of Japan''.Screech, Timon. (2006). ''Secret Memoirs of the Shoguns: Isaac Titsingh and Japan, 1779–1822'', p. 91. Tsunayoshi's first son Tokugawa Tokumatsu (1679–1683) died at the age of 4 due to illness. In 1704, Tsunayoshi's only surviving child, Tsuruhime died following a miscarriage and a few months after her{{whose|date=September 2024}} husband, his son-in-law, Tokugawa Tsunanori of [[:en:Kii Domain|Kii Domain]] also died. Therefore, Tsunayoshi appointed his nephew, [[:en:Tokugawa Ienobu|Tokugawa Ienobu]], heir apparent in the winter of 1704. Ienobu was the son of his other brother, [[:en:Tokugawa Tsunashige|Tokugawa Tsunashige]], the former Lord of [[:en:Kōfu|Kōfu]], which was a title Ienobu held himself before becoming ''shōgun''. Ienobu moved into the official residence of Shogunal heir apparent at the [[Edo_Castle#Ninomaru|Western Perimeter of Edo Castle]]. In 1706, Edo was hit by a typhoon, and [[:en:Mount Fuji|Mount Fuji]] erupted the following year. ==Death== It was insinuated that Tsunayoshi was stabbed by his consort after he tried to proclaim an illegitimate child as his heir; this concept, stemming from the [[Sanno Gaiki]], is refuted in contemporary records which explain that Tsunayoshi had the measles at the end of his life and died on February 19, 1709, in the presence of his entourage.Bodart-Bailey, p. 165. His death was just four days short of his 63rd birthday. He was given the Buddhist name Joken'in ({{lang|ja|常憲院}}) and buried in [[Kan'ei-ji]]. ==Eras of Tsunayoshi's ''bakufu''== The years in which Tsunayoshi was shogun are more specifically identified by more than one [[:en:Japanese era names|era name]] or ''[[:en:Nengō|Nengō]]''.Titsingh, pp. 414–415. * ''[[:en:Enpō|Enpō]]'' (1673–1681) * ''[[:en:Tenna|Tenna]]'' (1681–1684) * ''[[:en:Jōkyō|Jōkyō]]'' (1684–1688) * ''[[:en:Genroku|Genroku]]'' (1688–1704) * ''[[:en:Hōei|Hōei]]'' (1704–1711) ==Ancestry== {{ahnentafel |collapsed=yes |align=center |ref={{cite web|url=https://reichsarchiv.jp/%e5%ae%b6%e7%b3%bb%e3%83%aa%e3%82%b9%e3%83%88/%e5%be%b3%e5%b7%9d%ef%bc%88%e5%be%b7%e5%b7%9d%ef%bc%89%e6%b0%8f%ef%bc%88%e5%b0%86%e8%bb%8d%e5%ae%b6%ef%bc%89#tunayosi|title=Genealogy|website=Reichsarchiv|access-date=4 July 2018|language=ja}} |boxstyle_1=background-color: #fcc; |boxstyle_2=background-color: #fb9; |boxstyle_3=background-color: #ffc; |boxstyle_4=background-color: #bfc; |1= 1. (now [[:en:Tokyo|Tokyo]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]) | death_date = {{death date and age|1709|02|19|1646|02|23|df=y}} | death_place = Edo, Tokugawa shogunate | parents = [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]]
[[Keishouin]] | signature = Tokugawa Tsunayoshi kao.jpg | spouse = {{ill|Takatsukasa Nobuko|ja|鷹司信子|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takatsukasa Nobuko|qq=|1=Takatsukasa Nobuko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7140666}} }} {{family name hatnote|[[Tokugawa (surname)|Tokugawa]]|lang=Japanese}} {{nihongo|'''Tokugawa Tsunayoshi'''|徳川 綱吉||extra=February 23, 1646 – February 19, 1709}} was the fifth ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' of the [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa dynasty]] of Japan. He was the younger brother of [[:en:Tokugawa Ietsuna|Tokugawa Ietsuna]], as well as the son of [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]], the grandson of [[:en:Tokugawa Hidetada|Tokugawa Hidetada]], and the great-grandson of [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]].Nussbaum, Louis-Frédéric. (2005). "''Tokugawa, Tsunayoshi''" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|''Japan Encyclopedia'', p. 979|page=979}}; n.b., Louis-Frédéric is pseudonym of Louis-Frédéric Nussbaum, ''see'' [http://dispatch.opac.ddb.de/DB=4.1/PPN?PPN=128842709 Deutsche Nationalbibliothek Authority File] {{Webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20120524174828/http://dispatch.opac.ddb.de/DB=4.1/PPN?PPN=128842709 |date=2012-05-24 }}. Tsunayoshi is known for instituting animal protection laws, particularly for dogs. This earned him the nickname of "the dog ''Shogun''" (''Inu-Kubō'' 犬公方: ''Inu=''Dog, ''Kubō''=formal title of Shogun). ==Early years (1646–1680)== [[File:Keishōin.jpg|thumb|106px|Keishōin, Tsunayoshi's mother]] Tokugawa Tsunayoshi was born on February 23, 1646, in Edo. He was the son of [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]] by one of his concubines, named Otama, later known as Keishōin 桂昌院 (1627–1705). Tsunayoshi had an elder brother already five years old, who would become the next shogun after Iemitsu's death, [[:en:Tokugawa Ietsuna|Tokugawa Ietsuna]]. Tsunayoshi was born in [[:en:Edo|Edo]] and after his birth moved in with his mother to her own private apartments in [[:en:Edo Castle|Edo Castle]]. "The younger son (Tsunayoshi) apparently distinguished himself by his precociousness and liveliness at an early age, and the father, the third shogun, Iemitsu, became fearful that he might usurp the position of his duller elder brothers [and] thus he ordered that the boy (Tsunayoshi) not to be brought up as a samurai/warrior, as was becoming for his station, but be trained as a scholar."{{attribution needed|date=January 2018}}Bodart-Bailey, B., ed. (1999). ''Kaempfer's Japan: Tokugawa Japan Observed'', citing Buya shokudan, in Kokushi sosho, edited by Kokushi Kenkyu Kai (Tokyo 1917), ser. 2, 86–87. His childhood name was Tokumatsu ({{lang|ja|徳松}}). While his father was ''shōgun'', his mother was an adopted daughter of the [[Honjō family]], led by [[Honjō Munemasa]] (1580–1639) in Kyoto. His mother's natural parents were merchants in Kyoto. This remarkable woman was very close with Tsunayoshi in his young years, and while his older brother Ietsuna began to rely on regents for much of his reign, Tsunayoshi did exactly the opposite, relying on his remarkable mother for advice until her death. In 1651, ''shōgun'' Iemitsu died when Tsunayoshi was only five years old. His older brother, Tokugawa Ietsuna, became shogun. For the most part, Tsunayoshi's life during the reign of his brother ''shōgun'' Ietsuna is unknown, but he never advised his brother. ==Family== * Father: [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]] (August 12, 1604 – June 8, 1651) * Mother: Otama no Kata ({{lang|ja|玉方}},{{cite web |title=「桂昌院」の意味・読み・例文・類語 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%A1%82%E6%98%8C%E9%99%A2-16051 |website=コトバンク |date=13 May 2016 |publisher=日本国語大辞典 |access-date=28 October 2023}} 1627–1705) later {{ill|Keishōin|ja|桂昌院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keishōin|qq=|1=Keishōin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q5369704}}, daughter of {{ill|Honjo Munemasa|ja|本庄宗正|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honjo Munemasa|qq=|1=Honjō Munemasa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11520258}} * Wife: Takatsukasa Nobuko (1651–1709) later Jokoin, daughter of court noble [[:en:Takatsukasa Norihira|Takatsukasa Norihira]] * Concubines: ** Oden no Kata (1658–1738) later {{ill|Sheishin-in|ja|清心院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sheishin-in|qq=|1=Seishin'in|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11560633}} * Children: ** Tsuruhime (1677–1704) by Oden, married Tokugawa Tsunanori of [[:en:Kii Domain|Kii Domain]] ** Tokugawa Tokumatsu (1679–1683), [[:en:Tatebayashi Domain|Tatebayashi Domain]] by Oden * Adopted: ** [[:en:Tokugawa Ienobu|Tokugawa Ienobu]] ** Kichihime (1697–1701) signed as Midaidokoro's daughter ** Yaehime (1689–1746) daughter of [[:en:Takatsukasa Sukenobu|Takatsukasa Sukenobu]], married [[Tokugawa Yoshizane]] of Mito Family later Yousen-in had 1 daughter, Miyohime married [[:en:Tokugawa Munetaka|Tokugawa Munetaka]] signed as Midaidokoro's daughter ** Matsuhime daughter of [[:en:Tokugawa Tsunanari|Tokugawa Tsunanari]] married [[:en:Maeda Yoshinori|Maeda Yoshinori]] signed as Midaidokoro's daughter ** Takehime (1705–1772), daughter of Hirosada Seikan'in and adopted by [[:en:Tokugawa Yoshimune|Tokugawa Yoshimune]] and married [[Shimazu Tsugutoyo]] of [[:en:Satsuma Domain|Satsuma Domain]] and known as Joganin had 1 daughter, Kikuhime (1733–1808) signed as Midaidokoro's daughter and signed as Okume no Kata's daughter when she became adopted daughter of Yoshimune ==Disputed succession (1680)== In 1680, ''shōgun'' Ietsuna died at the premature age of 38. * '''June 4, 1680''' (''[[:en:Enpō|Enpō]] 8, 8th day of the 5th month''): Shogun Ietsuna's death leads to the accession of Tsunayoshi as head of the shogunate.Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). ''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 414. * '''1680–81''' (''Enpō 8''): [[:en:Gokoku-ji|Gokoku-ji]] in Edo is founded in honor of Tsunayoshi's mother. * '''1681''' (''[[:en:Tenna|Tenna]] 1''): Tsunayoshi's investiture as ''shōgun''. A power struggle ensued, and for a time, the succession remained an open question. [[:en:Sakai Tadakiyo|Sakai Tadakiyo]], one of Ietsuna's most favored advisors, suggested that the succession not pass to someone of the Tokugawa line, but rather to the blood royal, favoring one of the sons of [[:en:Emperor Go-Sai|Emperor Go-Sai]] to become the next ''shōgun'' (as during the [[:en:Kamakura shogunate|Kamakura shogunate]]) but Tadakiyo was dismissed soon after. [[:en:Hotta Masatoshi|Hotta Masatoshi]], one of the most brilliant advisors of ''shōgun'' Ietsuna's rule, was the first person to suggest that Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, as the brother of the former ''shōgun'' and the son of the third, become the next ''shōgun''. Finally, in 1681 (''Tenna 1''), Tsunayoshi's elevation was confirmed; and he was installed as the fifth ''shōgun'' of the Tokugawa shogunate. ==''Shōgun'' (1680–1709)== {{Unreferenced section|date=December 2022}} Immediately after becoming ''shōgun'', Tsunayoshi gave [[:en:Hotta Masatoshi|Hotta Masatoshi]] the title of ''[[:en:Tairō|Tairō]]'', in a way thanking him for ensuring his succession. Almost immediately after he became shogun, he ordered a vassal of the [[:en:Takada Domain|Takata]] to commit suicide because of misgovernment, showing his strict approach to the samurai code. He then confiscated his fief of 250,000 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]''. During his reign, he confiscated a total of 1,400,000 ''koku''. In 1682, ''shōgun'' Tsunayoshi ordered his censors and police to raise the living standard of the people. Soon, prostitution was banned, waitresses could not be employed in tea houses, and rare and expensive fabrics were banned. Most probably, smuggling began as a practice in Japan soon after Tsunayoshi's authoritarian laws came into effect. In 1684, Tsunayoshi also decreased the power of the ''tairō'' after the assassination of Masatoshi by a cousin in that same year. Nonetheless, due again to maternal advice, Tsunayoshi became very religious, promoting the [[:en:Neo-Confucianism|Neo-Confucianism]] of [[:en:Zhu Xi|Zhu Xi]]. In 1682, he read to the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]s'' an exposition of the "Great Learning", which became an annual tradition at the ''shōgun''{{'}}s court. He soon began to lecture even more, and in 1690 lectured about Neo-Confucian work to [[Shinto]] and [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] ''daimyōs'', and even to envoys from the court of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Higashiyama|Higashiyama]] in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. He also was interested in several Chinese works, namely ''The Great Learning'' ([[:en:Da Xue|Da Xue]]) and ''The Classic of Filial Piety'' ([[:en:Xiao Jing|Xiao Jing]]). Tsunayoshi also loved art and [[:en:Noh|Noh]] theater. In 1691, [[:en:Engelbert Kaempfer|Engelbert Kaempfer]] visited Edo as part of the annual [[:en:Dutch missions to Edo|Dutch embassy]] from [[:en:Dejima|Dejima]] in [[:en:Nagasaki|Nagasaki]]. He journeyed from Nagasaki to [[:en:Osaka|Osaka]], to [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], and there to [[:en:Edo|Edo]]. Kaempfer gives us information on Japan during the early reign of Tokugawa Tsunayoshi. As the Dutch embassy entered Edo in 1692, they asked to have an audience with Shogun Tsunayoshi. While they were waiting for approval, a fire destroyed six hundred houses in Edo, and the audience was postponed. Tsunayoshi and several of the ladies of the court sat behind reed screens, while the Dutch embassy sat in front of them. Tsunayoshi took an interest in Western matters, and apparently asked them to talk and sing with one another for him to see how Westerners behaved. Tsunayoshi later put on a Noh drama for them. [[File:Nakano Inugoya dog shelters 1696.png|thumb|Nakano Inugoya (Nakano dog shelters) in 1696. Tsunayoshi built large kennels in Nakano, Yotsuya and Okubo in Edo (Tokyo). Even during the famine the Shogunate accommodated 80,000 wild dogs in the kennels in Nakano and gave them 3 go (0.18L) of polished rice, 50 moon (187g) of bean paste and 1 go of sardines daily. The total space for the dog shelters in Nakano was approximately 750,000 square meters in 1702.[https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1178647/63 中野犬小屋本論]『武蔵野歴史地理. 第2冊』高橋源一郎編, 武蔵野歴史地理学会, 1928, p58-96]] Owing to religious fundamentalism, Tsunayoshi sought protection for living beings in the later parts of his rule. In the 1690s and first decade of the 1700s, Tsunayoshi, who was born in the Year of the Dog, thought he should take several measures concerning dogs. A collection of edicts released daily, known as the {{nihongo|''Edicts on Compassion for Living Things''|生類憐みの令|Shōruiawareminorei|}}, told the populace, among other things, to protect dogs, since in Edo there were many stray and diseased dogs walking around the city. Therefore, he earned the pejorative title ''Inu-Kubō'' (犬公方: ''Inu=''Dog, ''Kubō''=formal title of Shogun). In 1695, there were so many dogs that Edo began to smell horribly. An apprentice was even executed because he wounded a dog. Finally, the issue was taken to an extreme, as over 50,000 dogs were deported to kennels in the suburbs of the city where they would be housed. They were apparently fed rice and fish at the expense of the taxpaying citizens of Edo. For the latter part of Tsunayoshi's reign, he was advised by [[:en:Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu|Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu]]. It was a golden era of classic Japanese art, known as the ''[[:en:Genroku|Genroku]] era''. In 1701, [[:en:Asano Naganori|Asano Naganori]], the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Akō Domain|Akō]] han, having been allegedly insulted by [[:en:Kira Yoshinaka|Kira Yoshinaka]] in [[:en:Edo Castle|Edo Castle]], attempted to kill him. Asano was executed, but Kira went unpunished. Asano's [[:en:Forty-seven rōnin|forty-seven ''rōnin'']] avenged his death by killing Kira and became a legend that influenced many plays and stories of the era. The most successful of them was a [[:en:Bunraku|Bunraku]] play called ''Kanadehon Chūshingura'' (now simply called ''[[:en:Chūshingura|Chūshingura]]'', or "Treasury of Loyal Retainers"), written in 1748 by [[Takeda Izumo]] and two associates; it was later adapted into a [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] play, which is still one of Japan's most popular. The earliest known account of the Akō incident in the West was published in 1822 in [[:en:Isaac Titsingh|Isaac Titsingh]]'s book, ''Illustrations of Japan''.Screech, Timon. (2006). ''Secret Memoirs of the Shoguns: Isaac Titsingh and Japan, 1779–1822'', p. 91. Tsunayoshi's first son Tokugawa Tokumatsu (1679–1683) died at the age of 4 due to illness. In 1704, Tsunayoshi's only surviving child, Tsuruhime died following a miscarriage and a few months after her{{whose|date=September 2024}} husband, his son-in-law, Tokugawa Tsunanori of [[:en:Kii Domain|Kii Domain]] also died. Therefore, Tsunayoshi appointed his nephew, [[:en:Tokugawa Ienobu|Tokugawa Ienobu]], heir apparent in the winter of 1704. Ienobu was the son of his other brother, [[:en:Tokugawa Tsunashige|Tokugawa Tsunashige]], the former Lord of [[:en:Kōfu|Kōfu]], which was a title Ienobu held himself before becoming ''shōgun''. Ienobu moved into the official residence of Shogunal heir apparent at the [[Edo_Castle#Ninomaru|Western Perimeter of Edo Castle]]. In 1706, Edo was hit by a typhoon, and [[:en:Mount Fuji|Mount Fuji]] erupted the following year. ==Death== It was insinuated that Tsunayoshi was stabbed by his consort after he tried to proclaim an illegitimate child as his heir; this concept, stemming from the [[Sanno Gaiki]], is refuted in contemporary records which explain that Tsunayoshi had the measles at the end of his life and died on February 19, 1709, in the presence of his entourage.Bodart-Bailey, p. 165. His death was just four days short of his 63rd birthday. He was given the Buddhist name Joken'in ({{lang|ja|常憲院}}) and buried in [[Kan'ei-ji]]. ==Eras of Tsunayoshi's ''bakufu''== The years in which Tsunayoshi was shogun are more specifically identified by more than one [[:en:Japanese era names|era name]] or ''[[:en:Nengō|Nengō]]''.Titsingh, pp. 414–415. * ''[[:en:Enpō|Enpō]]'' (1673–1681) * ''[[:en:Tenna|Tenna]]'' (1681–1684) * ''[[:en:Jōkyō|Jōkyō]]'' (1684–1688) * ''[[:en:Genroku|Genroku]]'' (1688–1704) * ''[[:en:Hōei|Hōei]]'' (1704–1711) ==Ancestry== {{ahnentafel |collapsed=yes |align=center |ref={{cite web|url=https://reichsarchiv.jp/%e5%ae%b6%e7%b3%bb%e3%83%aa%e3%82%b9%e3%83%88/%e5%be%b3%e5%b7%9d%ef%bc%88%e5%be%b7%e5%b7%9d%ef%bc%89%e6%b0%8f%ef%bc%88%e5%b0%86%e8%bb%8d%e5%ae%b6%ef%bc%89#tunayosi|title=Genealogy|website=Reichsarchiv|access-date=4 July 2018|language=ja}} |boxstyle_1=background-color: #fcc; |boxstyle_2=background-color: #fb9; |boxstyle_3=background-color: #ffc; |boxstyle_4=background-color: #bfc; |1= 1. (now [[:en:Tokyo|Tokyo]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]) | death_date = {{death date and age|1709|02|19|1646|02|23|df=y}} | death_place = Edo, Tokugawa shogunate | parents = [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]]
[[Keishouin]] | signature = Tokugawa Tsunayoshi kao.jpg | spouse = {{ill|Takatsukasa Nobuko|ja|鷹司信子|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takatsukasa Nobuko|qq=|1=Takatsukasa Nobuko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7140666}} }} {{family name hatnote|[[Tokugawa (surname)|Tokugawa]]|lang=Japanese}} {{nihongo|'''Tokugawa Tsunayoshi'''|徳川 綱吉||extra=February 23, 1646 – February 19, 1709}} was the fifth ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' of the [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa dynasty]] of Japan. He was the younger brother of [[:en:Tokugawa Ietsuna|Tokugawa Ietsuna]], as well as the son of [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]], the grandson of [[:en:Tokugawa Hidetada|Tokugawa Hidetada]], and the great-grandson of [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]].Nussbaum, Louis-Frédéric. (2005). "''Tokugawa, Tsunayoshi''" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|''Japan Encyclopedia'', p. 979|page=979}}; n.b., Louis-Frédéric is pseudonym of Louis-Frédéric Nussbaum, ''see'' [http://dispatch.opac.ddb.de/DB=4.1/PPN?PPN=128842709 Deutsche Nationalbibliothek Authority File] {{Webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20120524174828/http://dispatch.opac.ddb.de/DB=4.1/PPN?PPN=128842709 |date=2012-05-24 }}. Tsunayoshi is known for instituting animal protection laws, particularly for dogs. This earned him the nickname of "the dog ''Shogun''" (''Inu-Kubō'' 犬公方: ''Inu=''Dog, ''Kubō''=formal title of Shogun). ==Early years (1646–1680)== [[File:Keishōin.jpg|thumb|106px|Keishōin, Tsunayoshi's mother]] Tokugawa Tsunayoshi was born on February 23, 1646, in Edo. He was the son of [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]] by one of his concubines, named Otama, later known as Keishōin 桂昌院 (1627–1705). Tsunayoshi had an elder brother already five years old, who would become the next shogun after Iemitsu's death, [[:en:Tokugawa Ietsuna|Tokugawa Ietsuna]]. Tsunayoshi was born in [[:en:Edo|Edo]] and after his birth moved in with his mother to her own private apartments in [[:en:Edo Castle|Edo Castle]]. "The younger son (Tsunayoshi) apparently distinguished himself by his precociousness and liveliness at an early age, and the father, the third shogun, Iemitsu, became fearful that he might usurp the position of his duller elder brothers [and] thus he ordered that the boy (Tsunayoshi) not to be brought up as a samurai/warrior, as was becoming for his station, but be trained as a scholar."{{attribution needed|date=January 2018}}Bodart-Bailey, B., ed. (1999). ''Kaempfer's Japan: Tokugawa Japan Observed'', citing Buya shokudan, in Kokushi sosho, edited by Kokushi Kenkyu Kai (Tokyo 1917), ser. 2, 86–87. His childhood name was Tokumatsu ({{lang|ja|徳松}}). While his father was ''shōgun'', his mother was an adopted daughter of the [[Honjō family]], led by [[Honjō Munemasa]] (1580–1639) in Kyoto. His mother's natural parents were merchants in Kyoto. This remarkable woman was very close with Tsunayoshi in his young years, and while his older brother Ietsuna began to rely on regents for much of his reign, Tsunayoshi did exactly the opposite, relying on his remarkable mother for advice until her death. In 1651, ''shōgun'' Iemitsu died when Tsunayoshi was only five years old. His older brother, Tokugawa Ietsuna, became shogun. For the most part, Tsunayoshi's life during the reign of his brother ''shōgun'' Ietsuna is unknown, but he never advised his brother. ==Family== * Father: [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]] (August 12, 1604 – June 8, 1651) * Mother: Otama no Kata ({{lang|ja|玉方}},{{cite web |title=「桂昌院」の意味・読み・例文・類語 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%A1%82%E6%98%8C%E9%99%A2-16051 |website=コトバンク |date=13 May 2016 |publisher=日本国語大辞典 |access-date=28 October 2023}} 1627–1705) later {{ill|Keishōin|ja|桂昌院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keishōin|qq=|1=Keishōin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q5369704}}, daughter of {{ill|Honjo Munemasa|ja|本庄宗正|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honjo Munemasa|qq=|1=Honjō Munemasa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11520258}} * Wife: Takatsukasa Nobuko (1651–1709) later Jokoin, daughter of court noble [[:en:Takatsukasa Norihira|Takatsukasa Norihira]] * Concubines: ** Oden no Kata (1658–1738) later {{ill|Zuishun-in|ja|瑞春院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zuishun-in|qq=|1=Zuishun'in|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7004392}} ** {{ill|Lady Emonosuke|ja|寿光院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lady Emonosuke|qq=}} (d. 1705) ** Lady Osuke (d. 1714) later Jukoin ** Lady Shinsuke, later {{ill|Sheishin-in|ja|清心院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sheishin-in|qq=|1=Seishin'in|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11560633}} * Children: ** Tsuruhime (1677–1704) by Oden, married Tokugawa Tsunanori of [[:en:Kii Domain|Kii Domain]] ** Tokugawa Tokumatsu (1679–1683), [[:en:Tatebayashi Domain|Tatebayashi Domain]] by Oden * Adopted: ** [[:en:Tokugawa Ienobu|Tokugawa Ienobu]] ** Kichihime (1697–1701) signed as Midaidokoro's daughter ** Yaehime (1689–1746) daughter of [[:en:Takatsukasa Sukenobu|Takatsukasa Sukenobu]], married [[Tokugawa Yoshizane]] of Mito Family later Yousen-in had 1 daughter, Miyohime married [[:en:Tokugawa Munetaka|Tokugawa Munetaka]] signed as Midaidokoro's daughter ** Matsuhime daughter of [[:en:Tokugawa Tsunanari|Tokugawa Tsunanari]] married [[:en:Maeda Yoshinori|Maeda Yoshinori]] signed as Midaidokoro's daughter ** Takehime (1705–1772), daughter of Hirosada Seikan'in and adopted by [[:en:Tokugawa Yoshimune|Tokugawa Yoshimune]] and married [[Shimazu Tsugutoyo]] of [[:en:Satsuma Domain|Satsuma Domain]] and known as Joganin had 1 daughter, Kikuhime (1733–1808) signed as Midaidokoro's daughter and signed as Okume no Kata's daughter when she became adopted daughter of Yoshimune ==Disputed succession (1680)== In 1680, ''shōgun'' Ietsuna died at the premature age of 38. * '''June 4, 1680''' (''[[:en:Enpō|Enpō]] 8, 8th day of the 5th month''): Shogun Ietsuna's death leads to the accession of Tsunayoshi as head of the shogunate.Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). ''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 414. * '''1680–81''' (''Enpō 8''): [[:en:Gokoku-ji|Gokoku-ji]] in Edo is founded in honor of Tsunayoshi's mother. * '''1681''' (''[[:en:Tenna|Tenna]] 1''): Tsunayoshi's investiture as ''shōgun''. A power struggle ensued, and for a time, the succession remained an open question. [[:en:Sakai Tadakiyo|Sakai Tadakiyo]], one of Ietsuna's most favored advisors, suggested that the succession not pass to someone of the Tokugawa line, but rather to the blood royal, favoring one of the sons of [[:en:Emperor Go-Sai|Emperor Go-Sai]] to become the next ''shōgun'' (as during the [[:en:Kamakura shogunate|Kamakura shogunate]]) but Tadakiyo was dismissed soon after. [[:en:Hotta Masatoshi|Hotta Masatoshi]], one of the most brilliant advisors of ''shōgun'' Ietsuna's rule, was the first person to suggest that Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, as the brother of the former ''shōgun'' and the son of the third, become the next ''shōgun''. Finally, in 1681 (''Tenna 1''), Tsunayoshi's elevation was confirmed; and he was installed as the fifth ''shōgun'' of the Tokugawa shogunate. ==''Shōgun'' (1680–1709)== {{Unreferenced section|date=December 2022}} Immediately after becoming ''shōgun'', Tsunayoshi gave [[:en:Hotta Masatoshi|Hotta Masatoshi]] the title of ''[[:en:Tairō|Tairō]]'', in a way thanking him for ensuring his succession. Almost immediately after he became shogun, he ordered a vassal of the [[:en:Takada Domain|Takata]] to commit suicide because of misgovernment, showing his strict approach to the samurai code. He then confiscated his fief of 250,000 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]''. During his reign, he confiscated a total of 1,400,000 ''koku''. In 1682, ''shōgun'' Tsunayoshi ordered his censors and police to raise the living standard of the people. Soon, prostitution was banned, waitresses could not be employed in tea houses, and rare and expensive fabrics were banned. Most probably, smuggling began as a practice in Japan soon after Tsunayoshi's authoritarian laws came into effect. In 1684, Tsunayoshi also decreased the power of the ''tairō'' after the assassination of Masatoshi by a cousin in that same year. Nonetheless, due again to maternal advice, Tsunayoshi became very religious, promoting the [[:en:Neo-Confucianism|Neo-Confucianism]] of [[:en:Zhu Xi|Zhu Xi]]. In 1682, he read to the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]s'' an exposition of the "Great Learning", which became an annual tradition at the ''shōgun''{{'}}s court. He soon began to lecture even more, and in 1690 lectured about Neo-Confucian work to [[Shinto]] and [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] ''daimyōs'', and even to envoys from the court of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Higashiyama|Higashiyama]] in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. He also was interested in several Chinese works, namely ''The Great Learning'' ([[:en:Da Xue|Da Xue]]) and ''The Classic of Filial Piety'' ([[:en:Xiao Jing|Xiao Jing]]). Tsunayoshi also loved art and [[:en:Noh|Noh]] theater. In 1691, [[:en:Engelbert Kaempfer|Engelbert Kaempfer]] visited Edo as part of the annual [[:en:Dutch missions to Edo|Dutch embassy]] from [[:en:Dejima|Dejima]] in [[:en:Nagasaki|Nagasaki]]. He journeyed from Nagasaki to [[:en:Osaka|Osaka]], to [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], and there to [[:en:Edo|Edo]]. Kaempfer gives us information on Japan during the early reign of Tokugawa Tsunayoshi. As the Dutch embassy entered Edo in 1692, they asked to have an audience with Shogun Tsunayoshi. While they were waiting for approval, a fire destroyed six hundred houses in Edo, and the audience was postponed. Tsunayoshi and several of the ladies of the court sat behind reed screens, while the Dutch embassy sat in front of them. Tsunayoshi took an interest in Western matters, and apparently asked them to talk and sing with one another for him to see how Westerners behaved. Tsunayoshi later put on a Noh drama for them. [[File:Nakano Inugoya dog shelters 1696.png|thumb|Nakano Inugoya (Nakano dog shelters) in 1696. Tsunayoshi built large kennels in Nakano, Yotsuya and Okubo in Edo (Tokyo). Even during the famine the Shogunate accommodated 80,000 wild dogs in the kennels in Nakano and gave them 3 go (0.18L) of polished rice, 50 moon (187g) of bean paste and 1 go of sardines daily. The total space for the dog shelters in Nakano was approximately 750,000 square meters in 1702.[https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1178647/63 中野犬小屋本論]『武蔵野歴史地理. 第2冊』高橋源一郎編, 武蔵野歴史地理学会, 1928, p58-96]] Owing to religious fundamentalism, Tsunayoshi sought protection for living beings in the later parts of his rule. In the 1690s and first decade of the 1700s, Tsunayoshi, who was born in the Year of the Dog, thought he should take several measures concerning dogs. A collection of edicts released daily, known as the {{nihongo|''Edicts on Compassion for Living Things''|生類憐みの令|Shōruiawareminorei|}}, told the populace, among other things, to protect dogs, since in Edo there were many stray and diseased dogs walking around the city. Therefore, he earned the pejorative title ''Inu-Kubō'' (犬公方: ''Inu=''Dog, ''Kubō''=formal title of Shogun). In 1695, there were so many dogs that Edo began to smell horribly. An apprentice was even executed because he wounded a dog. Finally, the issue was taken to an extreme, as over 50,000 dogs were deported to kennels in the suburbs of the city where they would be housed. They were apparently fed rice and fish at the expense of the taxpaying citizens of Edo. For the latter part of Tsunayoshi's reign, he was advised by [[:en:Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu|Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu]]. It was a golden era of classic Japanese art, known as the ''[[:en:Genroku|Genroku]] era''. In 1701, [[:en:Asano Naganori|Asano Naganori]], the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Akō Domain|Akō]] han, having been allegedly insulted by [[:en:Kira Yoshinaka|Kira Yoshinaka]] in [[:en:Edo Castle|Edo Castle]], attempted to kill him. Asano was executed, but Kira went unpunished. Asano's [[:en:Forty-seven rōnin|forty-seven ''rōnin'']] avenged his death by killing Kira and became a legend that influenced many plays and stories of the era. The most successful of them was a [[:en:Bunraku|Bunraku]] play called ''Kanadehon Chūshingura'' (now simply called ''[[:en:Chūshingura|Chūshingura]]'', or "Treasury of Loyal Retainers"), written in 1748 by [[Takeda Izumo]] and two associates; it was later adapted into a [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] play, which is still one of Japan's most popular. The earliest known account of the Akō incident in the West was published in 1822 in [[:en:Isaac Titsingh|Isaac Titsingh]]'s book, ''Illustrations of Japan''.Screech, Timon. (2006). ''Secret Memoirs of the Shoguns: Isaac Titsingh and Japan, 1779–1822'', p. 91. Tsunayoshi's first son Tokugawa Tokumatsu (1679–1683) died at the age of 4 due to illness. In 1704, Tsunayoshi's only surviving child, Tsuruhime died following a miscarriage and a few months after her{{whose|date=September 2024}} husband, his son-in-law, Tokugawa Tsunanori of [[:en:Kii Domain|Kii Domain]] also died. Therefore, Tsunayoshi appointed his nephew, [[:en:Tokugawa Ienobu|Tokugawa Ienobu]], heir apparent in the winter of 1704. Ienobu was the son of his other brother, [[:en:Tokugawa Tsunashige|Tokugawa Tsunashige]], the former Lord of [[:en:Kōfu|Kōfu]], which was a title Ienobu held himself before becoming ''shōgun''. Ienobu moved into the official residence of Shogunal heir apparent at the [[Edo_Castle#Ninomaru|Western Perimeter of Edo Castle]]. In 1706, Edo was hit by a typhoon, and [[:en:Mount Fuji|Mount Fuji]] erupted the following year. ==Death== It was insinuated that Tsunayoshi was stabbed by his consort after he tried to proclaim an illegitimate child as his heir; this concept, stemming from the [[Sanno Gaiki]], is refuted in contemporary records which explain that Tsunayoshi had the measles at the end of his life and died on February 19, 1709, in the presence of his entourage.Bodart-Bailey, p. 165. His death was just four days short of his 63rd birthday. He was given the Buddhist name Joken'in ({{lang|ja|常憲院}}) and buried in [[Kan'ei-ji]]. ==Eras of Tsunayoshi's ''bakufu''== The years in which Tsunayoshi was shogun are more specifically identified by more than one [[:en:Japanese era names|era name]] or ''[[:en:Nengō|Nengō]]''.Titsingh, pp. 414–415. * ''[[:en:Enpō|Enpō]]'' (1673–1681) * ''[[:en:Tenna|Tenna]]'' (1681–1684) * ''[[:en:Jōkyō|Jōkyō]]'' (1684–1688) * ''[[:en:Genroku|Genroku]]'' (1688–1704) * ''[[:en:Hōei|Hōei]]'' (1704–1711) ==Ancestry== {{ahnentafel |collapsed=yes |align=center |ref={{cite web|url=https://reichsarchiv.jp/%e5%ae%b6%e7%b3%bb%e3%83%aa%e3%82%b9%e3%83%88/%e5%be%b3%e5%b7%9d%ef%bc%88%e5%be%b7%e5%b7%9d%ef%bc%89%e6%b0%8f%ef%bc%88%e5%b0%86%e8%bb%8d%e5%ae%b6%ef%bc%89#tunayosi|title=Genealogy|website=Reichsarchiv|access-date=4 July 2018|language=ja}} |boxstyle_1=background-color: #fcc; |boxstyle_2=background-color: #fb9; |boxstyle_3=background-color: #ffc; |boxstyle_4=background-color: #bfc; |1= 1. (now [[:en:Tokyo|Tokyo]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]) | death_date = {{death date and age|1709|02|19|1646|02|23|df=y}} | death_place = Edo, Tokugawa shogunate | parents = [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]]
[[Keishouin]] | signature = Tokugawa Tsunayoshi kao.jpg | spouse = {{ill|Takatsukasa Nobuko|ja|鷹司信子|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takatsukasa Nobuko|qq=|1=Takatsukasa Nobuko|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7140666}} }} {{family name hatnote|[[Tokugawa (surname)|Tokugawa]]|lang=Japanese}} {{nihongo|'''Tokugawa Tsunayoshi'''|徳川 綱吉||extra=February 23, 1646 – February 19, 1709}} was the fifth ''[[:en:Shogun|Shogun]]'' of the [[Tokugawa shogunate|Tokugawa dynasty]] of Japan. He was the younger brother of [[:en:Tokugawa Ietsuna|Tokugawa Ietsuna]], as well as the son of [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]], the grandson of [[:en:Tokugawa Hidetada|Tokugawa Hidetada]], and the great-grandson of [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]].Nussbaum, Louis-Frédéric. (2005). "''Tokugawa, Tsunayoshi''" in {{Google books|p2QnPijAEmEC|''Japan Encyclopedia'', p. 979|page=979}}; n.b., Louis-Frédéric is pseudonym of Louis-Frédéric Nussbaum, ''see'' [http://dispatch.opac.ddb.de/DB=4.1/PPN?PPN=128842709 Deutsche Nationalbibliothek Authority File] {{Webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20120524174828/http://dispatch.opac.ddb.de/DB=4.1/PPN?PPN=128842709 |date=2012-05-24 }}. Tsunayoshi is known for instituting animal protection laws, particularly for dogs. This earned him the nickname of "the dog ''Shogun''" (''Inu-Kubō'' 犬公方: ''Inu=''Dog, ''Kubō''=formal title of Shogun). ==Early years (1646–1680)== [[File:Keishōin.jpg|thumb|106px|Keishōin, Tsunayoshi's mother]] Tokugawa Tsunayoshi was born on February 23, 1646, in Edo. He was the son of [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]] by one of his concubines, named Otama, later known as Keishōin 桂昌院 (1627–1705). Tsunayoshi had an elder brother already five years old, who would become the next shogun after Iemitsu's death, [[:en:Tokugawa Ietsuna|Tokugawa Ietsuna]]. Tsunayoshi was born in [[:en:Edo|Edo]] and after his birth moved in with his mother to her own private apartments in [[:en:Edo Castle|Edo Castle]]. "The younger son (Tsunayoshi) apparently distinguished himself by his precociousness and liveliness at an early age, and the father, the third shogun, Iemitsu, became fearful that he might usurp the position of his duller elder brothers [and] thus he ordered that the boy (Tsunayoshi) not to be brought up as a samurai/warrior, as was becoming for his station, but be trained as a scholar."{{attribution needed|date=January 2018}}Bodart-Bailey, B., ed. (1999). ''Kaempfer's Japan: Tokugawa Japan Observed'', citing Buya shokudan, in Kokushi sosho, edited by Kokushi Kenkyu Kai (Tokyo 1917), ser. 2, 86–87. His childhood name was Tokumatsu ({{lang|ja|徳松}}). While his father was ''shōgun'', his mother was an adopted daughter of the [[Honjō family]], led by [[Honjō Munemasa]] (1580–1639) in Kyoto. His mother's natural parents were merchants in Kyoto. This remarkable woman was very close with Tsunayoshi in his young years, and while his older brother Ietsuna began to rely on regents for much of his reign, Tsunayoshi did exactly the opposite, relying on his remarkable mother for advice until her death. In 1651, ''shōgun'' Iemitsu died when Tsunayoshi was only five years old. His older brother, Tokugawa Ietsuna, became shogun. For the most part, Tsunayoshi's life during the reign of his brother ''shōgun'' Ietsuna is unknown, but he never advised his brother. ==Family== * Father: [[:en:Tokugawa Iemitsu|Tokugawa Iemitsu]] (August 12, 1604 – June 8, 1651) * Mother: Otama no Kata ({{lang|ja|玉方}},{{cite web |title=「桂昌院」の意味・読み・例文・類語 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%A1%82%E6%98%8C%E9%99%A2-16051 |website=コトバンク |date=13 May 2016 |publisher=日本国語大辞典 |access-date=28 October 2023}} 1627–1705) later {{ill|Keishōin|ja|桂昌院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keishōin|qq=|1=Keishōin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q5369704}}, daughter of {{ill|Honjo Munemasa|ja|本庄宗正|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Honjo Munemasa|qq=|1=Honjō Munemasa|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11520258}} * Wife: Takatsukasa Nobuko (1651–1709) later Jokoin, daughter of court noble [[:en:Takatsukasa Norihira|Takatsukasa Norihira]] * Concubines: ** Oden no Kata (1658–1738) later {{ill|Zuishun-in|ja|瑞春院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Zuishun-in|qq=|1=Zuishun'in|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q7004392}} ** {{ill|Lady Emonosuke|ja|寿光院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Lady Emonosuke|qq=}} (d. 1705) ** Lady Osuke (d. 1714) later Jukoin ** Lady Shinsuke, later {{ill|Sheishin-in|ja|清心院|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sheishin-in|qq=|1=Seishin'in|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11560633}} * Children: ** Tsuruhime (1677–1704) by Oden, married Tokugawa Tsunanori of [[:en:Kii Domain|Kii Domain]] ** Tokugawa Tokumatsu (1679–1683), [[:en:Tatebayashi Domain|Tatebayashi Domain]] by Oden * Adopted: ** [[:en:Tokugawa Ienobu|Tokugawa Ienobu]] ** Kichihime (1697–1701) signed as Midaidokoro's daughter ** Yaehime (1689–1746) daughter of [[:en:Takatsukasa Sukenobu|Takatsukasa Sukenobu]], married [[Tokugawa Yoshizane]] of Mito Family later Yousen-in had 1 daughter, Miyohime married [[:en:Tokugawa Munetaka|Tokugawa Munetaka]] signed as Midaidokoro's daughter ** Matsuhime daughter of [[:en:Tokugawa Tsunanari|Tokugawa Tsunanari]] married [[:en:Maeda Yoshinori|Maeda Yoshinori]] signed as Midaidokoro's daughter ** Takehime (1705–1772), daughter of Hirosada Seikan'in and adopted by [[:en:Tokugawa Yoshimune|Tokugawa Yoshimune]] and married [[Shimazu Tsugutoyo]] of [[:en:Satsuma Domain|Satsuma Domain]] and known as Joganin had 1 daughter, Kikuhime (1733–1808) signed as Midaidokoro's daughter and signed as Okume no Kata's daughter when she became adopted daughter of Yoshimune ==Disputed succession (1680)== In 1680, ''shōgun'' Ietsuna died at the premature age of 38. * '''June 4, 1680''' (''[[:en:Enpō|Enpō]] 8, 8th day of the 5th month''): Shogun Ietsuna's death leads to the accession of Tsunayoshi as head of the shogunate.Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). ''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 414. * '''1680–81''' (''Enpō 8''): [[:en:Gokoku-ji|Gokoku-ji]] in Edo is founded in honor of Tsunayoshi's mother. * '''1681''' (''[[:en:Tenna|Tenna]] 1''): Tsunayoshi's investiture as ''shōgun''. A power struggle ensued, and for a time, the succession remained an open question. [[:en:Sakai Tadakiyo|Sakai Tadakiyo]], one of Ietsuna's most favored advisors, suggested that the succession not pass to someone of the Tokugawa line, but rather to the blood royal, favoring one of the sons of [[:en:Emperor Go-Sai|Emperor Go-Sai]] to become the next ''shōgun'' (as during the [[:en:Kamakura shogunate|Kamakura shogunate]]) but Tadakiyo was dismissed soon after. [[:en:Hotta Masatoshi|Hotta Masatoshi]], one of the most brilliant advisors of ''shōgun'' Ietsuna's rule, was the first person to suggest that Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, as the brother of the former ''shōgun'' and the son of the third, become the next ''shōgun''. Finally, in 1681 (''Tenna 1''), Tsunayoshi's elevation was confirmed; and he was installed as the fifth ''shōgun'' of the Tokugawa shogunate. ==''Shōgun'' (1680–1709)== {{Unreferenced section|date=December 2022}} Immediately after becoming ''shōgun'', Tsunayoshi gave [[:en:Hotta Masatoshi|Hotta Masatoshi]] the title of ''[[:en:Tairō|Tairō]]'', in a way thanking him for ensuring his succession. Almost immediately after he became shogun, he ordered a vassal of the [[:en:Takada Domain|Takata]] to commit suicide because of misgovernment, showing his strict approach to the samurai code. He then confiscated his fief of 250,000 ''[[:en:Koku|Koku]]''. During his reign, he confiscated a total of 1,400,000 ''koku''. In 1682, ''shōgun'' Tsunayoshi ordered his censors and police to raise the living standard of the people. Soon, prostitution was banned, waitresses could not be employed in tea houses, and rare and expensive fabrics were banned. Most probably, smuggling began as a practice in Japan soon after Tsunayoshi's authoritarian laws came into effect. In 1684, Tsunayoshi also decreased the power of the ''tairō'' after the assassination of Masatoshi by a cousin in that same year. Nonetheless, due again to maternal advice, Tsunayoshi became very religious, promoting the [[:en:Neo-Confucianism|Neo-Confucianism]] of [[:en:Zhu Xi|Zhu Xi]]. In 1682, he read to the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]s'' an exposition of the "Great Learning", which became an annual tradition at the ''shōgun''{{'}}s court. He soon began to lecture even more, and in 1690 lectured about Neo-Confucian work to [[Shinto]] and [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] ''daimyōs'', and even to envoys from the court of Emperor [[:en:Emperor Higashiyama|Higashiyama]] in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]]. He also was interested in several Chinese works, namely ''The Great Learning'' ([[:en:Da Xue|Da Xue]]) and ''The Classic of Filial Piety'' ([[:en:Xiao Jing|Xiao Jing]]). Tsunayoshi also loved art and [[:en:Noh|Noh]] theater. In 1691, [[:en:Engelbert Kaempfer|Engelbert Kaempfer]] visited Edo as part of the annual [[:en:Dutch missions to Edo|Dutch embassy]] from [[:en:Dejima|Dejima]] in [[:en:Nagasaki|Nagasaki]]. He journeyed from Nagasaki to [[:en:Osaka|Osaka]], to [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], and there to [[:en:Edo|Edo]]. Kaempfer gives us information on Japan during the early reign of Tokugawa Tsunayoshi. As the Dutch embassy entered Edo in 1692, they asked to have an audience with Shogun Tsunayoshi. While they were waiting for approval, a fire destroyed six hundred houses in Edo, and the audience was postponed. Tsunayoshi and several of the ladies of the court sat behind reed screens, while the Dutch embassy sat in front of them. Tsunayoshi took an interest in Western matters, and apparently asked them to talk and sing with one another for him to see how Westerners behaved. Tsunayoshi later put on a Noh drama for them. [[File:Nakano Inugoya dog shelters 1696.png|thumb|Nakano Inugoya (Nakano dog shelters) in 1696. Tsunayoshi built large kennels in Nakano, Yotsuya and Okubo in Edo (Tokyo). Even during the famine the Shogunate accommodated 80,000 wild dogs in the kennels in Nakano and gave them 3 go (0.18L) of polished rice, 50 moon (187g) of bean paste and 1 go of sardines daily. The total space for the dog shelters in Nakano was approximately 750,000 square meters in 1702.[https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1178647/63 中野犬小屋本論]『武蔵野歴史地理. 第2冊』高橋源一郎編, 武蔵野歴史地理学会, 1928, p58-96]] Owing to religious fundamentalism, Tsunayoshi sought protection for living beings in the later parts of his rule. In the 1690s and first decade of the 1700s, Tsunayoshi, who was born in the Year of the Dog, thought he should take several measures concerning dogs. A collection of edicts released daily, known as the {{nihongo|''Edicts on Compassion for Living Things''|生類憐みの令|Shōruiawareminorei|}}, told the populace, among other things, to protect dogs, since in Edo there were many stray and diseased dogs walking around the city. Therefore, he earned the pejorative title ''Inu-Kubō'' (犬公方: ''Inu=''Dog, ''Kubō''=formal title of Shogun). In 1695, there were so many dogs that Edo began to smell horribly. An apprentice was even executed because he wounded a dog. Finally, the issue was taken to an extreme, as over 50,000 dogs were deported to kennels in the suburbs of the city where they would be housed. They were apparently fed rice and fish at the expense of the taxpaying citizens of Edo. For the latter part of Tsunayoshi's reign, he was advised by [[:en:Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu|Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu]]. It was a golden era of classic Japanese art, known as the ''[[:en:Genroku|Genroku]] era''. In 1701, [[:en:Asano Naganori|Asano Naganori]], the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of [[:en:Akō Domain|Akō]] han, having been allegedly insulted by [[:en:Kira Yoshinaka|Kira Yoshinaka]] in [[:en:Edo Castle|Edo Castle]], attempted to kill him. Asano was executed, but Kira went unpunished. Asano's [[:en:Forty-seven rōnin|forty-seven ''rōnin'']] avenged his death by killing Kira and became a legend that influenced many plays and stories of the era. The most successful of them was a [[:en:Bunraku|Bunraku]] play called ''Kanadehon Chūshingura'' (now simply called ''[[:en:Chūshingura|Chūshingura]]'', or "Treasury of Loyal Retainers"), written in 1748 by [[Takeda Izumo]] and two associates; it was later adapted into a [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] play, which is still one of Japan's most popular. The earliest known account of the Akō incident in the West was published in 1822 in [[:en:Isaac Titsingh|Isaac Titsingh]]'s book, ''Illustrations of Japan''.Screech, Timon. (2006). ''Secret Memoirs of the Shoguns: Isaac Titsingh and Japan, 1779–1822'', p. 91. Tsunayoshi's first son Tokugawa Tokumatsu (1679–1683) died at the age of 4 due to illness. In 1704, Tsunayoshi's only surviving child, Tsuruhime died following a miscarriage and a few months after her{{whose|date=September 2024}} husband, his son-in-law, Tokugawa Tsunanori of [[:en:Kii Domain|Kii Domain]] also died. Therefore, Tsunayoshi appointed his nephew, [[:en:Tokugawa Ienobu|Tokugawa Ienobu]], heir apparent in the winter of 1704. Ienobu was the son of his other brother, [[:en:Tokugawa Tsunashige|Tokugawa Tsunashige]], the former Lord of [[:en:Kōfu|Kōfu]], which was a title Ienobu held himself before becoming ''shōgun''. Ienobu moved into the official residence of Shogunal heir apparent at the [[Edo_Castle#Ninomaru|Western Perimeter of Edo Castle]]. In 1706, Edo was hit by a typhoon, and [[:en:Mount Fuji|Mount Fuji]] erupted the following year. ==Death== It was insinuated that Tsunayoshi was stabbed by his consort after he tried to proclaim an illegitimate child as his heir; this concept, stemming from the [[Sanno Gaiki]], is refuted in contemporary records which explain that Tsunayoshi had the measles at the end of his life and died on February 19, 1709, in the presence of his entourage.Bodart-Bailey, p. 165. His death was just four days short of his 63rd birthday. He was given the Buddhist name Joken'in ({{lang|ja|常憲院}}) and buried in [[Kan'ei-ji]]. ==Eras of Tsunayoshi's ''bakufu''== The years in which Tsunayoshi was shogun are more specifically identified by more than one [[:en:Japanese era names|era name]] or ''[[:en:Nengō|Nengō]]''.Titsingh, pp. 414–415. * ''[[:en:Enpō|Enpō]]'' (1673–1681) * ''[[:en:Tenna|Tenna]]'' (1681–1684) * ''[[:en:Jōkyō|Jōkyō]]'' (1684–1688) * ''[[:en:Genroku|Genroku]]'' (1688–1704) * ''[[:en:Hōei|Hōei]]'' (1704–1711) ==Ancestry== {{ahnentafel |collapsed=yes |align=center |ref={{cite web|url=https://reichsarchiv.jp/%e5%ae%b6%e7%b3%bb%e3%83%aa%e3%82%b9%e3%83%88/%e5%be%b3%e5%b7%9d%ef%bc%88%e5%be%b7%e5%b7%9d%ef%bc%89%e6%b0%8f%ef%bc%88%e5%b0%86%e8%bb%8d%e5%ae%b6%ef%bc%89#tunayosi|title=Genealogy|website=Reichsarchiv|access-date=4 July 2018|language=ja}} |boxstyle_1=background-color: #fcc; |boxstyle_2=background-color: #fb9; |boxstyle_3=background-color: #ffc; |boxstyle_4=background-color: #bfc; |1= 1.
