Yoshimune ==Disputed succession (1680)== In 1680, ''shōgun'' Ietsuna died at the premature age of 38. * '''June 4, 1680''' (''{{ill|Enpō|en|Enpō|WD=Q1145735|lt=Enpō|1=Enpō}} 8, 8th day of the 5th month''): Shogun Ietsuna's death leads to the accession of Tsunayoshi as head of the shogunate.Titsingh, Isaac. (1834). ''Annales des empereurs du japon,'' p. 414. * '''1680–81''' (''Enpō 8''): {{ill|Gokoku-ji|en|Gokoku-ji|WD=Q1534481|lt=Gokoku-ji|1=Gokoku-ji}} in Edo is founded in honor of Tsunayoshi's mother. * '''1681''' (''{{ill|Tenna|en|Tenna|WD=Q1145289|lt=Tenna|1=Tenna}} 1''): Tsunayoshi's investiture as ''shōgun''. A power struggle ensued, and for a time, the succession remained an open question. {{ill|Sakai Tadakiyo|en|Sakai Tadakiyo|WD=Q7402769|lt=Sakai Tadakiyo|1=Sakai Tadakiyo}}, one of Ietsuna's most favored advisors, suggested that the succession not pass to someone of the Tokugawa line, but rather to the blood royal, favoring one of the sons of {{ill|Emperor Go-Sai|en|Emperor Go-Sai|WD=Q349414|lt=Emperor Go-Sai|1=Emperor Go-Sai}} to become the next ''shōgun'' (as during the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|en|Kamakura shogunate|WD=Q736839|lt=Kamakura shogunate|1=Kamakura shogunate}}) but Tadakiyo was dismissed soon after. {{ill|Hotta Masatoshi|en|Hotta Masatoshi|WD=Q936047|lt=Hotta Masatoshi|1=Hotta Masatoshi}}, one of the most brilliant advisors of ''shōgun'' Ietsuna's rule, was the first person to suggest that Tokugawa Tsunayoshi, as the brother of the former ''shōgun'' and the son of the third, become the next ''shōgun''. Finally, in 1681 (''Tenna 1''), Tsunayoshi's elevation was confirmed; and he was installed as the fifth ''shōgun'' of the Tokugawa shogunate. ==''Shōgun'' (1680–1709)== {{Unreferenced section|date=December 2022}} Immediately after becoming ''shōgun'', Tsunayoshi gave {{ill|Hotta Masatoshi|en|Hotta Masatoshi|WD=Q936047|lt=Hotta Masatoshi|1=Hotta Masatoshi}} the title of ''{{ill|Tairō|en|Tairō|WD=Q956844|lt=Tairō|1=Tairō}}'', in a way thanking him for ensuring his succession. Almost immediately after he became shogun, he ordered a vassal of the {{ill|Takada Domain|en|Takada Domain|WD=Q839422|lt=Takata|1=Takada Domain}} to commit suicide because of misgovernment, showing his strict approach to the samurai code. He then confiscated his fief of 250,000 ''{{ill|Koku|en|Koku|WD=Q855048|lt=Koku|1=Koku}}''. During his reign, he confiscated a total of 1,400,000 ''koku''. In 1682, ''shōgun'' Tsunayoshi ordered his censors and police to raise the living standard of the people. Soon, prostitution was banned, waitresses could not be employed in tea houses, and rare and expensive fabrics were banned. Most probably, smuggling began as a practice in Japan soon after Tsunayoshi's authoritarian laws came into effect. In 1684, Tsunayoshi also decreased the power of the ''tairō'' after the assassination of Masatoshi by a cousin in that same year. Nonetheless, due again to maternal advice, Tsunayoshi became very religious, promoting the {{ill|Neo-Confucianism|en|Neo-Confucianism|WD=Q825754|lt=Neo-Confucianism|1=Neo-Confucianism}} of {{ill|Zhu Xi|en|Zhu Xi|WD=Q9397|lt=Zhu Xi|1=Zhu Xi}}. In 1682, he read to the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]s'' an exposition of the "Great Learning", which became an annual tradition at the ''shōgun''{{'}}s court. He soon began to lecture even more, and in 1690 lectured about Neo-Confucian work to [[Shinto]] and {{ill|Buddhism|en|Buddhism|WD=Q748|lt=Buddhism|1=Buddhism}} ''daimyōs'', and even to envoys from the court of Emperor {{ill|Emperor Higashiyama|en|Emperor Higashiyama|WD=Q313801|lt=Higashiyama|1=Emperor Higashiyama}} in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}}. He also was interested in several Chinese works, namely ''The Great Learning'' ([[:en:Da Xue|Da Xue]]) and ''The Classic of Filial Piety'' ([[:en:Xiao Jing|Xiao Jing]]). Tsunayoshi also loved art and {{ill|Noh|en|Noh|WD=Q226887|lt=Noh|1=Noh}} theater. In 1691, {{ill|Engelbert Kaempfer|en|Engelbert Kaempfer|WD=Q58042|lt=Engelbert Kaempfer|1=Engelbert Kaempfer}} visited Edo as part of the annual {{ill|Dutch missions to Edo|en|Dutch missions to Edo|WD=Q1411432|lt=Dutch embassy|1=Dutch missions to Edo}} from {{ill|Dejima|en|Dejima|WD=Q640267|lt=Dejima|1=Dejima}} in {{ill|Nagasaki|en|Nagasaki|WD=Q38234|lt=Nagasaki|1=Nagasaki}}. He journeyed from Nagasaki to {{ill|Osaka|en|Osaka|WD=Q35765|lt=Osaka|1=Osaka}}, to {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|WD=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}}, and there to {{ill|Edo|en|Edo|WD=Q215646|lt=Edo|1=Edo}}. Kaempfer gives us information on Japan during the early reign of Tokugawa Tsunayoshi. As the Dutch embassy entered Edo in 1692, they asked to have an audience with Shogun Tsunayoshi. While they were waiting for approval, a fire destroyed six hundred houses in Edo, and the audience was postponed. Tsunayoshi and several of the ladies of the court sat behind reed screens, while the Dutch embassy sat in front of them. Tsunayoshi took an interest in Western matters, and apparently asked them to talk and sing with one another for him to see how Westerners behaved. Tsunayoshi later put on a Noh drama for them. [[File:Nakano Inugoya dog shelters 1696.png|thumb|Nakano Inugoya (Nakano dog shelters) in 1696. Tsunayoshi built large kennels in Nakano, Yotsuya and Okubo in Edo (Tokyo). Even during the famine the Shogunate accommodated 80,000 wild dogs in the kennels in Nakano and gave them 3 go (0.18L) of polished rice, 50 moon (187g) of bean paste and 1 go of sardines daily. The total space for the dog shelters in Nakano was approximately 750,000 square meters in 1702.[https://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1178647/63 中野犬小屋本論]『武蔵野歴史地理. 第2冊』高橋源一郎編, 武蔵野歴史地理学会, 1928, p58-96]] Owing to religious fundamentalism, Tsunayoshi sought protection for living beings in the later parts of his rule. In the 1690s and first decade of the 1700s, Tsunayoshi, who was born in the Year of the Dog, thought he should take several measures concerning dogs. A collection of edicts released daily, known as the {{nihongo|''Edicts on Compassion for Living Things''|生類憐みの令|Shōruiawareminorei|}}, told the populace, among other things, to protect dogs, since in Edo there were many stray and diseased dogs walking around the city. Therefore, he earned the pejorative title ''Inu-Kubō'' (犬公方: ''Inu=''Dog, ''Kubō''=formal title of Shogun). In 1695, there were so many dogs that Edo began to smell horribly. An apprentice was even executed because he wounded a dog. Finally, the issue was taken to an extreme, as over 50,000 dogs were deported to kennels in the suburbs of the city where they would be housed. They were apparently fed rice and fish at the expense of the taxpaying citizens of Edo. For the latter part of Tsunayoshi's reign, he was advised by {{ill|Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu|en|Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu|WD=Q846911|lt=Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu|1=Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu}}. It was a golden era of classic Japanese art, known as the ''{{ill|Genroku|en|Genroku|WD=Q1325001|lt=Genroku|1=Genroku}} era''. In 1701, {{ill|Asano Naganori|en|Asano Naganori|WD=Q2866316|lt=Asano Naganori|1=Asano Naganori}}, the ''[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]'' of {{ill|Akō Domain|en|Akō Domain|WD=Q1062196|lt=Akō|1=Akō Domain}} han, having been allegedly insulted by {{ill|Kira Yoshinaka|en|Kira Yoshinaka|WD=Q3132109|lt=Kira Yoshinaka|1=Kira Yoshinaka}} in {{ill|Edo Castle|en|Edo Castle|WD=Q865913|lt=Edo Castle|1=Edo Castle}}, attempted to kill him. Asano was executed, but Kira went unpunished. Asano's {{ill|Forty-seven rōnin|en|Forty-seven rōnin|WD=Q822472|lt=forty-seven ''rōnin''|1=Forty-seven rōnin}} avenged his death by killing Kira and became a legend that influenced many plays and stories of the era. The most successful of them was a {{ill|Bunraku|en|Bunraku|WD=Q243170|lt=Bunraku|1=Bunraku}} play called ''Kanadehon Chūshingura'' (now simply called ''{{ill|Chūshingura|en|Chūshingura|WD=Q683379|lt=Chūshingura|1=Chūshingura}}'', or "Treasury of Loyal Retainers"), written in 1748 by [[Takeda Izumo]] and two associates; it was later adapted into a {{ill|Kabuki|en|Kabuki|WD=Q199701|lt=Kabuki|1=Kabuki}} play, which is still one of Japan's most popular. The earliest known account of the Akō incident in the West was published in 1822 in {{ill|Isaac Titsingh|en|Isaac Titsingh|WD=Q332779|lt=Isaac Titsingh|1=Isaac Titsingh}}'s book, ''Illustrations of Japan''.Screech, Timon. (2006). ''Secret Memoirs of the Shoguns: Isaac Titsingh and Japan, 1779–1822'', p. 91. Tsunayoshi's first son Tokugawa Tokumatsu (1679–1683) died at the age of 4 due to illness. In 1704, Tsunayoshi's only surviving child, Tsuruhime died following a miscarriage and a few months after her{{whose|date=September 2024}} husband, his son-in-law, Tokugawa Tsunanori of [[:en:Kii Domain|Kii Domain]] also died. Therefore, Tsunayoshi appointed his nephew, {{ill|Tokugawa Ienobu|en|Tokugawa Ienobu|WD=Q366734|lt=Tokugawa Ienobu|1=Tokugawa Ienobu}}, heir apparent in the winter of 1704. Ienobu was the son of his other brother, {{ill|Tokugawa Tsunashige|en|Tokugawa Tsunashige|WD=Q7004484|lt=Tokugawa Tsunashige|1=Tokugawa Tsunashige}}, the former Lord of {{ill|Kōfu|en|Kōfu|WD=Q201932|lt=Kōfu|1=Kōfu}}, which was a title Ienobu held himself before becoming ''shōgun''. Ienobu moved into the official residence of Shogunal heir apparent at the [[Edo_Castle#Ninomaru|Western Perimeter of Edo Castle]]. In 1706, Edo was hit by a typhoon, and {{ill|Mount Fuji|en|Mount Fuji|WD=Q39231|lt=Mount Fuji|1=Mount Fuji}} erupted the following year. ==Death== It was insinuated that Tsunayoshi was stabbed by his consort after he tried to proclaim an illegitimate child as his heir; this concept, stemming from the [[Sanno Gaiki]], is refuted in contemporary records which explain that Tsunayoshi had the measles at the end of his life and died on February 19, 1709, in the presence of his entourage.Bodart-Bailey, p. 165. His death was just four days short of his 63rd birthday. He was given the Buddhist name Joken'in ({{lang|ja|常憲院}}) and buried in [[Kan'ei-ji]]. ==Eras of Tsunayoshi's ''bakufu''== The years in which Tsunayoshi was shogun are more specifically identified by more than one [[:en:Japanese era names|era name]] or ''[[:en:Nengō|Nengō]]''.Titsingh, pp. 414–415. * ''{{ill|Enpō|en|Enpō|WD=Q1145735|lt=Enpō|1=Enpō}}'' (1673–1681) * ''{{ill|Tenna|en|Tenna|WD=Q1145289|lt=Tenna|1=Tenna}}'' (1681–1684) * ''{{ill|Jōkyō|en|Jōkyō|WD=Q1146221|lt=Jōkyō|1=Jōkyō}}'' (1684–1688) * ''{{ill|Genroku|en|Genroku|WD=Q1325001|lt=Genroku|1=Genroku}}'' (1688–1704) * ''{{ill|Hōei|en|Hōei|WD=Q1145262|lt=Hōei|1=Hōei}}'' (1704–1711) ==Ancestry== {{ahnentafel |collapsed=yes |align=center |ref={{cite web|url=https://reichsarchiv.jp/%e5%ae%b6%e7%b3%bb%e3%83%aa%e3%82%b9%e3%83%88/%e5%be%b3%e5%b7%9d%ef%bc%88%e5%be%b7%e5%b7%9d%ef%bc%89%e6%b0%8f%ef%bc%88%e5%b0%86%e8%bb%8d%e5%ae%b6%ef%bc%89#tunayosi|title=Genealogy|website=Reichsarchiv|access-date=4 July 2018|language=ja}} |boxstyle_1=background-color: #fcc; |boxstyle_2=background-color: #fb9; |boxstyle_3=background-color: #ffc; |boxstyle_4=background-color: #bfc; |1= 1.
